transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I came in because I just can’t seem to settle anymore. It’s like I’m crawling around inside my own skin, if that makes sense. I’ll be worn out and know I should sit down, but then I’m up again doing the next thing, and then another thing.

It’s silly, I’ll sit in the chair and think, “Just stay here a minute,” and then I remember the kitchen or the laundry or something I saw on the table—anyway, it feels like I can’t be still inside, even when I’m tired.
Did this restless, can't-sit-still feeling start after you began a new medication or changed the dose of one?

I don’t know that I can tie it to a medicine change, no. I mean, I’d have to think about it—I’ve taken things here and there over the years, and sometimes the bottles all look the same if you don’t keep them straight. My daughter is always telling me to use one of those little pill boxes, but then I misplace the pill box, so that doesn’t help much.

But no, I don’t remember this starting right after a new pill or a dose change. At least nothing that stands out to me.
Have you been feeling unusually high, euphoric, or full of energy lately?

Unusually high? I don’t think so… I mean, not like happy-high or anything. Full of energy is funny because sometimes I’m moving around a lot, but it doesn’t feel good, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I’m suddenly cheerful and ready to take on the world.

I did have a neighbor once who would get like that—she’d be out in the yard at dawn planting things, and I’d think, my goodness, I can barely get my coffee made without setting something down and forgetting it. But no, I don’t think I’ve been euphoric or anything like that.
When you feel unable to settle, is it because a thought keeps bothering you until you get up and do something?

It’s not always one thought, no. Sometimes I couldn’t even tell you what it is I’m getting up for until I’m already halfway across the room. It’s more like this feeling inside, like I can’t settle in my own skin.

I’ll be worn out and think, “You need to sit down,” and then—there I go—up to do the next thing. And then I notice something else, and off I go again. My mother used to say I had ants in my pants as a girl, though I don’t know if that’s the same thing. But now it just feels exhausting, like I should be still and I just can’t quite stay there.
When you were a child, did you often have trouble sitting still?

Oh yes, I think so. I mean, I don’t remember every little thing from back then, of course, but I do remember my report cards saying things like I was bright but careless. My teachers were always writing that I lost papers or talked when I wasn’t supposed to.

And sitting still—yes, they’d remind me to stay in my seat or finish my work. I can still picture those little comments in the margins. Funny, my mother kept some of those papers in a box for years, mixed in with old birthday cards and things, but yes… that was definitely a problem even in grade school.
Have these problems with sitting still and getting distracted been present for most of your adult life too?

Well… I suppose I’ve always been a bit that way, but the real trouble with it, the part where it’s been getting in my way, has been since my husband died. That was about… a year and ten months ago now.

It’s funny, I still catch myself thinking I should tell him something, like where I put the grocery list, and then I remember. But yes, since then it’s been much harder to manage, the sitting still and getting distracted.
Since your husband died, have you been worrying a lot more than usual?

I don’t know if I’d call it worrying more than usual… maybe. I mean, after someone dies there are so many little things to think about, aren’t there? Forms and cupboards and whether you’ve paid the bill already, and I’ll put something down and then wonder where I put it.

But worry—hmm. I suppose I’m not sure what counts as “a lot.” Some days I’m just going from one thing to another and then I realize I’ve been thinking about something entirely different, like whether I left the kettle on, but then I was also thinking about the neighbor’s cat because it keeps coming into my garden. So… I’m not sure I can answer that cleanly.
Do you get upsetting thoughts that keep intruding into your mind even when you try not to think about them?

I’m not sure… I mean, thoughts come and go, don’t they? Sometimes something pops into my head when I’m trying to do the washing up or find my glasses, but I don’t know if I’d call them upsetting exactly.

It’s more like my mind wanders off on its own. Like I’ll start thinking about one thing and then suddenly I’m remembering I meant to clean out that drawer in the hall—the one with all the old batteries in it, which really shouldn’t be mixed together, my husband used to say that. But intrusive upsetting thoughts… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed that in a clear way.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things on most days?

Many different things… I’m not sure. I do think about a lot of things, but whether it’s worry-worry, I don’t know.

Some days I’ll be thinking about the post, then the garden, then whether I moved something in the kitchen, and it all sort of tumbles together. But “excessively” sounds like a big word. I don’t really know how to measure that.
Do you often feel unable to stop worrying once it starts?

I don’t really know. Sometimes I’ll have a thought and it sort of runs along for a bit, but then I’ll notice something else—like the laundry or a noise outside—and I’m off onto that instead.

So unable to stop… I’m not sure I’d put it that way. My mind doesn’t always feel very orderly, but whether that’s worry carrying on or just me getting sidetracked, I can’t quite tell.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports a longstanding pattern of hyperactivity/restlessness and distractibility beginning in childhood and persisting into adulthood, with functional impairment. The patient confirms childhood symptoms such as difficulty sitting still, talking out of turn, losing papers, careless schoolwork, and teacher comments to stay seated/finish work. In adulthood she continues to experience an inner sense of restlessness, inability to remain seated, distractibility, and task-switching. Symptoms worsened after her husband's death but clearly predated this stressor. Alternative explanations explored in the interview were not supported: no clear medication-triggered onset, no euphoric/manic state, no obsession-driven behavior, and no clearly excessive/uncontrollable generalized worry.
